chapter_theme: Under the heading உறவினர், nine verses on kin: one must feel dependants' trouble as one's own and feed them, good kin remove distress, stand by in trouble even after enmity and help at last like late rain, their hurtful counsel is to be borne, and one taken as kin follows his kinsman; but even brothers should not share a roof long, and dice among kin, as the Bharata shows, make them strangers.

348.reading: If a man does not feel that what befalls those who depend on him has befallen himself, as though it were his own, what is the use of him, for that is like pounding husk and getting only sore hands.
348.nuance: The verse doubles the identification: the dependants' trouble must be taken as one's own (தமக்குற்றதேயாக) and spoken of as 'ours' (எமக்குற்றது). Kinship without that feeling is not merely cold but wasted effort, which the proverb makes concrete. The hill-country address is a frame.

pazhamozhi.literal: like pounding chaff and only hurting one's hands

story.act: no story; the proverb names labour that yields nothing

pazhamozhi.applied_to: keeping dependants without sharing their trouble as one's own is fruitless toil

349.reading: Even if a man on whom others have come to depend trusts them as wholly his own, unless he sees that those he has chosen do not go in want, what way have they to go on, for all else is false and only cooked food is true.
349.nuance: The syntax of lines 1 to 3 is compressed and the sense of தீர்ந்தாரா and செல்லாமை is not certain; on the reading taken here, the patron's trust in his dependants' loyalty counts for nothing unless he feeds them, which is what the proverb's அட்டூண் (food that has been cooked) clinches.
349.domain_note: the man on whom kin depend

pazhamozhi.literal: everything is false; only food that has been cooked is true

story.act: no story; the proverb sets the meal actually served against every other profession

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a bond with dependants is proved by providing for them, not by trusting them

350.reading: When someone falls into distress, those called his good kin are the ones who remove it by the way of good deeds, and that is the medicine that has become a tree in one's own house.
350.nuance: The verse defines good kin by their act (வினைமரபின் ... நீக்கும்), not by birth; the proverb's tree growing in the house yard is a remedy that needs no search, so kin are help near at hand.

pazhamozhi.literal: the medicine that has grown as a tree of the house

story.act: no story; the proverb names a remedy growing at home

pazhamozhi.applied_to: good kin who remove one's distress are a remedy close at hand

351.reading: Taken truly, what do outsiders ever do for one another; but one's own people, even if they seem never to do anything, will do it, as rain, they say, will rain even when it has held off.
351.nuance: The contrast is between பிறர் (others) and தமர் (one's own). The proverb concedes the delay: kin, like rain, may fail for a season, but their help is certain in the end. The address to a woman is a frame.

pazhamozhi.literal: rain, they say, will rain even if it has not rained

story.act: no story; the proverb rests on the certainty of rain after a dry spell

pazhamozhi.applied_to: kin help in the end even when they seem to fail

352.reading: Those of one family, even if they were hostile before, stand behind a man and do not leave him when overwhelming trouble comes, while others will not come in even if he treats them as gold, for outsiders are not those who draw close.
352.nuance: முன்னின்னார் (unpleasant before) and பின்னின்னார் (standing behind afterwards) are a pun on the same syllables; the loyalty is owed to shared family (ஒருகுடியார்), not to past kindness, and the outsider's failure is set against favours given him (பொன்னாச் செயினும்).

pazhamozhi.literal: others are not the ones who draw near

story.act: no story; the proverb states the outsider's distance

pazhamozhi.applied_to: in trouble one's family closes in and strangers stay away

353.reading: Even if they speak so that it hurts, it is good to hear counsel for one's good from the mouths of kin, for a mother's treading does not make her young lame.
353.nuance: The address in line 3 (birds treading on flowers in the ripe fields) prepares the proverb's image of a mother bird treading her chicks. The hurt of kin's words is real (உளைய) but cannot cripple, because of who gives it.

pazhamozhi.literal: a mother's treading does not make one lame

story.act: no story; the proverb draws on a mother hen or bird treading on her young

pazhamozhi.applied_to: hurtful counsel from kin is to be heeded because it does no lasting harm

354.reading: When someone, valuing you, has taken you as his own, then whatever befalls, you do what he does, and what trouble is there in that, for the thread goes where the needle goes.
354.nuance: Who values whom in line 1 is not fixed; the reading here takes the subject of கொண்டக்கால் as the one who accepts and the addressee as the accepted kinsman who then follows him. The address in line 3 is to a man of the hills (இன்னொலி வெற்ப).

pazhamozhi.literal: the thread goes the way the sewing needle goes

story.act: no story; the proverb is the needle and thread

pazhamozhi.applied_to: one taken as kin follows his kinsman's course whatever it costs

355.reading: Even for those who mingled together in the womb, living long in one place together is painful, for sharing a dwelling is unpleasant even with Tiru who sits on the lotus.
355.nuance: The heading praises kin, and this verse turns: brothers born of one womb (கருவினுட் கொண்டு கலந்தாரும்) should not stay long under one roof. துச்சு is taken as a shared or borrowed dwelling; the proverb's goddess of fortune makes the point that even the best companion palls.

pazhamozhi.literal: sharing a dwelling is unpleasant even with the goddess of fortune

story.act: no story; the proverb names Tiru on the lotus as the most welcome of housemates

pazhamozhi.applied_to: even brothers should not live together long

356.reading: In the Bharata too, the twice fifty, staking their inheritance, faced the five in war, became strangers to them and broke apart; therefore one does not play dice with those one loves.
356.nuance: The verse reads the epic as a case about kin: the dice turned brothers' sons into ஏதிலர் (strangers). It does not name Dharma's loss but makes the stake their own share (தம் தாயமா).

pazhamozhi.literal: people do not play at dice with those they love

story.act: the hundred staked their inheritance at dice against the five, went to war with them and became strangers

links.note: Kural 521 says honouring old ties when all is lost is found only in kin; Pazhamozhi 352 extends it to kin who were hostile before, and sets them against outsiders who were favoured.
links.teaches: Together they show that kin loyalty in ruin does not rest on remembered kindness: even a hostile kinsman stands behind, so the bond is of family, not of debt.
links.list_adds: its contrast of ஒருகுடியார் with பிறர் treated as gold gives the couplet a counter-case, the favoured outsider who still will not come in.

links.note: Naladiyar 113 says that in trouble few kin claim the relation; Pazhamozhi 352 says those of one family do not part from a man in trouble.
links.teaches: On the same test, trouble, the two works give opposite verdicts on kin, one of shared family loyalty and one of kin as fair-weather clingers, so the ethics group has no settled view.
links.list_adds: it narrows kin to ஒருகுடியார் and puts the desertion on outsiders, where the quatrain puts it on kin themselves.

links.note: Naladiyar 203 says the great never refuse to bear those who depend on them; Pazhamozhi 348 says bearing them is useless unless their trouble is felt as one's own.
links.teaches: The pair adds an inner condition to the duty of support: carrying dependants as a branch carries fruit is not enough if their trouble is not felt as one's own.
links.list_adds: its proverb of pounding husk turns support without fellow feeling from a virtue into wasted labour.

links.note: Naladiyar 201 says a man's distress vanishes on seeing kin who ask after him; Pazhamozhi 350 says good kin are those who remove distress by deeds.
links.teaches: Read together, the comfort of kin has two measures, being asked after and being helped, and the Pazhamozhi verse ranks the deed as what makes kin good.
links.list_adds: it defines good kin by their act (வினைமரபின் நீக்கும்) and makes them a remedy at hand, where the quatrain heals by presence alone.

links.note: Nanmanikkadigai 3 says the use of kin is known when one is ruined; Pazhamozhi 350 says what that use is, removing the distress, and calls it a medicine at home.
links.teaches: The counted verse gives the test of kin and the proverb verse its content, so ruin both reveals kin and is the thing good kin cure.

links.note: Kural 529 says kin who left return when the cause of discord is gone; Pazhamozhi 351 says kin who seem never to help will help at last, as rain falls after holding off.
links.teaches: The couplet makes the return of kin wait on removing a cause, while the rain proverb makes it as sure as weather, so delay in kin's help is no proof of its absence.
links.list_adds: its rain proverb gives kin help the certainty of a natural cycle and sets it against strangers who never help.

links.note: Kural 448 says a ruler without those who rebuke him perishes; Pazhamozhi 353 says hurtful counsel should be heard from kin, whose treading, like a mother's, does not lame.
links.teaches: The pair moves the needed rebuker from the king's council into the family and gives a reason the couplet lacks for bearing him: the bond guarantees the hurt does no harm.
links.list_adds: its mother-bird proverb explains why rebuke is bearable, which the couplet only declares necessary.

links.note: Naladiyar 208 says true intimates enter the fire with you like the smith's poker; Pazhamozhi 354 says one taken as kin follows wherever his kinsman goes, as thread follows the needle.
links.teaches: Both use a craftsman's tool for loyalty, but the poker proves itself in danger and the thread by following, so kin loyalty is shown as obedience to another's course whatever it costs.
links.list_adds: its needle and thread make loyalty a matter of following the kinsman's lead, where the quatrain's smithy tools sort friends by their behaviour in the heat.

links.note: Kural 524 makes living surrounded by kin the fruit of wealth; Pazhamozhi 355 says even brothers living long in one dwelling is painful.
links.teaches: The pair separates being surrounded by kin from sharing a roof with them: the Kural's ideal holds only at a distance, for even brothers wear on one another at close quarters.
links.list_adds: its proverb that even the goddess of fortune is a bad housemate puts a limit of nearness and time on the couplet's praise.

links.note: Nanmanikkadigai 49 says living apart from one's companions is hard for the well-born; Pazhamozhi 355 says living long together in one place, even for brothers, is painful.
links.teaches: Held together, the two verses name a real dilemma of kinship: separation is hard and long cohabitation painful, so kin are best close but not under one roof.

links.note: Kural 938 lists what gambling destroys: wealth, truth, compassion; Pazhamozhi 356 shows by the Bharata that dice between kin destroy kinship itself.
links.teaches: The couplet's loss of compassion becomes, in the epic case, brothers' sons turned into strangers and enemies, so the worst stake at dice is the bond with the other player.
links.list_adds: its Bharata story names a loss the couplet's list leaves out, the player's kin turned ஏதிலர்.

links.note: Naladiyar 191 says kin live at ease on what their relative gives, like crops below a tank; Pazhamozhi 349 says the patron's trust in them means nothing unless he sees they do not go in want.
links.teaches: The pair makes provision the substance of the kin bond: the quatrain shows kin living on the giver, and the proverb verse denies that trust without the meal is any bond at all.
links.list_adds: its proverb that all is false but cooked food puts feeding above every other proof of kinship, which the quatrain assumes without arguing.
